title: Key Points on Overcoming Addiction
excerpt: Excerpt from Overcoming Addiction: Case Analysis and Self-Help Guide for Addiction Treatment

inline.s: Excerpt from Overcoming Addiction: Case Analysis and Self-Help Guide for Addiction Treatment
Keeping body and mind pure, joyful, and uplifted is vital to health, longevity, and happiness, yet addiction is a stumbling block in the way.

Addiction refers to a repetitive compulsive behavior — one that continues to be repeated even when the person knows it may bring harmful consequences (that is, one cannot control oneself). If you have a strong dependence on something, can gain temporary satisfaction from it, but feel utterly miserable and unable to stop when you cannot have it, then you are addicted.

I am a psychological expert in treating addiction, and I was once an addict myself. This distinctive experience has allowed me to develop a unique theory of addiction treatment and to help thousands upon thousands of addicts.

If a person is to change, he must first admit that he has certain problems and be willing to change. Addiction is not merely indulgence in drugs or alcohol; any substance or behavior you use to regulate your emotional state has the potential to addict you.

Church and charitable activities are, on the surface, positive activities. But in this case, Jean hoped subconsciously to use them to escape painful feelings and the handling of difficult problems. Only after three sessions did she admit that she in fact deeply resented her husband, because he was so often not at her side. Yet she had never communicated any of this to her husband — or to herself.

Compared with people, cigarettes, alcohol, or cookies are easier to grow dependent on, and they are readily available and can be controlled at will. Many addicts do not realize that they have substituted substances for connection between people.

For Kevin, marijuana enabled him to escape anxiety and depression. Fortunately, his girlfriend Denise was able to keep him in a state of sweetness and calm, taking over the role that marijuana had once played.

A shopping addict, after buying an expensive set of living-room furniture, will persuade himself that the new furniture can save his marriage or raise his social standing. For an addict, every feeling of excitement is worth questioning.
In my view, all forms of substance addiction are the same in essence — namely, using substitute substances to relieve feelings of depression and discomfort.
When an addict has several addictive behaviors at once, one must judge which of them is the most dangerous or most fatal.

To keep myself from eating ice cream is very difficult, because it would make me feel empty, anxious, or depressed. This behavior already meets the criteria of addiction, which is precisely why I want to quit it.

When a smoker is immersed in the calming effect of cigarettes, he temporarily forgets the unpleasant things in life and does not feel negative emotions such as distress, and so he will not come up with creative or constructive ways to solve the problems that actually exist. In the long run, this is not conducive to an individual’s emotional growth and success.

Generally speaking, the period when an addict has just begun to stop the addictive behavior is the most painful, yet in fact it is then that they are healthiest. And when they feel most comfortable and pleased, they are often the least clear-headed; at that time they are the sickest and most likely to harm themselves. Only by understanding the truth and facing the reality that “treatment is painful” can one be truly healed.

In addicts one often sees a paradoxical phenomenon. They very much long to be close to others, yet they often abandon people in favor of the addictive substance, because the latter is less likely to disappoint them and easier to control than people.

I have found that the more successful and wealthy a person is, the more people will tolerate antisocial behavior that harms his own mental health. Society, in accepting Jim’s eccentricities and immature behavior, has also done him great harm.

In more than thirty years of clinical practice, I have rarely seen an addict with only a single vice. Sometimes a drinker seems devoted only to alcohol, but if you uncover the surface, you will find that they usually also smoke or drink coffee every day. When their resistance is lowered by alcohol, they may develop sexual addiction or eating problems.

If left alone and untreated, addiction will grow ever more severe. The hidden distress behind it needs to be released and dealt with directly. Taken to the extreme, these seemingly benign behaviors — such as running, eating ice cream, attending worship — will take control of your life and endanger the rest.
Of the addicts I have seen,

have serious narcissistic tendencies. An addict’s degree of narcissism can be judged by the degree of his obsession with the addiction. From my experience, a narcissistic man cannot think clearly about what he hopes to get from a woman, and so a woman can never make him happy.

Lily enrolled in more courses and took a part-time job at a local bookstore. She replaced her dangerous compulsive behavior with something healthier, more meaningful, and more stable. In the end she completely stopped vomiting, gained a little weight, and then I began to suggest she attend a full-time school.

Relapse is an unavoidable part of addiction treatment. If a patient tells me he has relapsed into drug addiction, I do not blame him or get angry, nor do I merely acknowledge that it disappoints me. I want to make him believe that this is a very normal phenomenon, letting the patient feel understanding and deep care — which is in fact the best way to overcome drug addiction.

When he sat down on the sofa, I thought to myself: “He is going to kill me.” He was an alcoholic, but worse still, he had violent tendencies. I said to him: “If you want my help, you must first let me not be afraid of you. If you do not, I cannot carry out my work.”

Even if you do not want to be a champion drinker at holiday dinners and parties, you should not urge others to drink. Please remember that many people — including members of your family — lack tolerance for alcohol, and excessive drinking may harm innocent bystanders.

Sometimes, people who have successfully quit drugs, cigarettes, or alcohol for a period of time want to test themselves. They think: “If I face the tempting situation again, I will surely be able to resist the temptation.” But in fact, such tests often end in failure and may even bring about a relapse!
